sumber: KSSM Form 4 English DSKP (CEFR-aligned). All passages and questions are written for the app; medium to hard.

nota.t: Tenses show when an action happens. Present simple for habits and facts (She walks to school); present continuous for actions now (She is walking); present perfect for past actions linked to now (She has finished); past simple for completed past actions (She walked); past continuous for an action in progress in the past (She was walking when it rained); future with will or going to.
Example: I have lived here since 2020. (present perfect, still true now)

Conditionals: zero (If you heat ice, it melts — facts), first (If it rains, I will stay home — real future), second (If I were rich, I would travel — unreal present) and third (If I had studied, I would have passed — unreal past). Relative clauses add information using who (people), which (things), that, whose (possession) and where (places).
Relative clause: The girl who won the prize is my cousin.

Passive voice focuses on the action or receiver: be + past participle (The letter was written by Ali). Use it when the doer is unknown or unimportant. Reported speech changes tense back one step and changes pronouns and time words: 'I am tired,' she said → She said that she was tired.
Reported: 'I will come tomorrow,' he said → He said that he would come the next day.

d: Passive: The letter was written by Ali.

nota.t: Modals express ability (can, could), permission (may, can), obligation (must, have to), advice (should), possibility (might, may) and deduction (must be, can't be). Gerunds (-ing used as nouns) follow verbs like enjoy, avoid, finish; infinitives (to + verb) follow want, decide, hope. Some verbs take both with a change in meaning (stop smoking / stop to smoke).

r: He stopped to rest / stopped running.

t: Tenses, conditionals, relative clauses, passive, reported speech, modals, gerunds and infinitives.

nota.t: Phrasal verbs combine a verb with a particle to make a new meaning: give up (stop), look after (care for), run out of (have none left), put off (postpone), turn down (refuse). Idioms are fixed expressions with non-literal meanings: a piece of cake (easy), break the ice (start a conversation), hit the books (study hard).

Collocations are words that naturally go together: make a decision, do homework, heavy rain, strong coffee, take a photo. Word formation builds new words with prefixes (un-, dis-, im-, re-) and suffixes (-ness, -ment, -ful, -ly, -tion): happy → unhappy → happiness; decide → decision.

t: Phrasal verbs, idioms, collocations, word formation.

nota.t: Reading comprehension strategies: skim for the main idea, scan for specific details, use context clues for new words, identify the writer's purpose and tone, and infer meaning that is not stated directly. Support answers with evidence from the text.

Formal writing (letters of complaint, reports, articles for the school magazine) uses a clear structure, formal vocabulary, no contractions and polite tone. Informal writing (emails and letters to friends) is personal and conversational. Always consider purpose, audience and format.

Linkers connect ideas: addition (furthermore, moreover), contrast (however, although), cause and effect (therefore, as a result), sequence (firstly, finally) and example (for instance). A good paragraph has a topic sentence, supporting details with examples, and a concluding sentence.

t: Formal and informal register; linkers; paragraphs; emails, letters, articles, reports.

nota.t: Literature in action: study poems and prose for theme, characters, setting, plot, point of view, language and moral values. Explain literary devices such as imagery, metaphor, simile, personification and symbolism, and link the text to your own life.

t: Poetry and prose terms: theme, persona, tone, imagery, plot, conflict.
